segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: ‘Thus says the one who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know your works, your toil and your endurance, and that you cannot bear evil people. You have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and you have found them false.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You have endurance, and you have borne up for the sake of my name, and have not grown weary.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I have this against you: you have abandoned the love you had at first.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Remember, then, from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first. If not, I am coming to you, and I will move your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But this you do have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the churches. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And to the angel of the church in Smyrna write: ‘Thus says the first and the last, who was dead and came to life:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know your affliction and your poverty—though you are rich—and the slander from those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not be afraid of what you are about to suffer. Look, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison so that you may be tested, and you will have affliction for ten days. Be faithful to the point of death, and I will give you the crown of life.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the churches. The one who conquers will certainly not be harmed by the second death.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And to the angel of the church in Pergamum write: ‘Thus says the one who has the sharp two-edged sword:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know where you live, where Satan’s throne is. Yet you hold fast to my name, and you did not deny your faith in me even in the days of Antipas, my witness, my faithful one, who was killed among you, where Satan lives.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold fast to the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, to eat food sacrificed to idols and to commit sexual immorality.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In the same way you too have some who hold fast to the teaching of the Nicolaitans.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Repent, then. If not, I am coming to you soon, and I will make war against them with the sword of my mouth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write: ‘Thus says the Son of God, whose eyes are like a flame of fire and whose feet are like burnished bronze:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know your works—your love and faith and service and endurance—and that your last works are greater than the first.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I have this against you: you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophet; she teaches and leads my slaves astray, to commit sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I gave her time to repent, but she is not willing to repent of her sexual immorality.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look, I am throwing her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her into great affliction, unless they repent of her works;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and I will kill her children with pestilence. Then all the churches will know that I am the one who searches minds and hearts, and I will give to each of you according to your works.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But to the rest of you in Thyatira, all who do not hold this teaching, who have not come to know the deep things of Satan, as they call them—to you I say: I lay no other burden on you;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: only hold fast to what you have until I come.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And the one who conquers and keeps my works until the end—to that one I will give authority over the nations,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: to shepherd them with an iron rod, as clay pots are smashed to pieces,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: just as I also have received it from my Father. And I will give that one the morning star.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the churches.’

notes.note: The Greek word means ‘messenger’ and can refer to a human envoy or a heavenly being. Some interpreters take the ‘angel’ of each church to be its human leader or the courier of the letter. Because the word everywhere else in Revelation refers to heavenly beings, most scholars understand a heavenly representative or counterpart of the congregation, and the traditional rendering is kept.

Nothing certain is known about this group beyond what this chapter says. Verses 14–15 link their teaching with eating food offered to idols and sexual immorality, which suggests they encouraged Christians to accommodate themselves to pagan civic and religious life. Later church writers connected them with the Nicolaus of Acts 6:5, but that link is unverified.

The phrase reflects a local conflict in Smyrna between the Christ-followers and a synagogue community that, in John’s view, was denouncing them, perhaps to the civic authorities. John, himself Jewish, treats ‘Jew’ as a title of honour and disputes his opponents’ right to it. This is the language of a first-century dispute over who belongs to Israel, not a description of Jewish people generally.

The Greek word denotes the wreath awarded to victorious athletes and to honoured citizens, not a monarch’s crown, for which Revelation uses a different word. ‘Crown’ is kept in its sense of a victor’s garland. The image is of a prize given to the one who finishes the contest, the prize being life itself.

Pergamum was a leading centre of Roman administration and of emperor worship in the province of Asia, and also housed a monumental altar of Zeus and a famous sanctuary of Asclepius. Which of these, if any single one, John has in mind is disputed. Many scholars favour the imperial cult, since refusal to take part in it was a likely cause of Antipas’s death.
The Greek is literally ‘my faith’. It is taken here as faith directed toward Christ, as in most modern versions. It could also mean loyalty to him.

The verb covers unlawful sexual conduct in general. In the prophets of Israel it is also a standard image for religious unfaithfulness, and many scholars think that here and in verses 20–21 it refers mainly or wholly to participation in idolatrous worship. The allusion is to Numbers 25 and 31:16, where Israel’s men are drawn into both sexual relations and idol-feasts on Balaam’s advice. The literal rendering is kept so that both readings remain open.

The word means a pebble or small stone such as was used for casting votes, a white one signifying acquittal. Stones or tokens also served as admission tickets and as amulets inscribed with names. No single explanation of the image has won general agreement; a token of acquittal or of admission to the heavenly banquet are the commonest proposals.

This Greek word is found only here and in 1:15, and its exact meaning is unknown. It clearly names some high-quality copper alloy, bronze or brass, and the context in 1:15 suggests metal glowing or gleaming. Thyatira was known for its metalworkers, so the term may have been a local trade word.

The Greek word ordinarily meant a slave, a person owned by a master, and that is what a first-century reader would have heard. English versions have traditionally softened it to ‘servants’. In biblical usage, being God’s slave is also a title of honour borne by Moses and the prophets, expressing total belonging.

Jezebel was the queen who promoted the worship of Baal in Israel (1 Kings 16–21). The name is almost certainly a symbolic label for an influential woman teacher in Thyatira, not her real name. Some manuscripts read ‘your wife Jezebel’, but the shorter reading is generally preferred.

The Greek says simply ‘a bed’. To be thrown onto a bed is a Semitic way of speaking of being struck with illness, and most modern versions make this explicit. The plain word may also carry an ironic contrast with the bed of adultery or the dining couch of an idol-feast.

notes.traditional: I will strike her children dead
notes.note: The Greek is literally ‘kill with death’. In the Greek Old Testament ‘death’ regularly translates the Hebrew word for plague, and Revelation 6:8 uses it the same way, so ‘pestilence’ is likely what readers understood. Most English versions instead take the phrase as an emphatic idiom, ‘strike dead’. ‘Her children’ probably means her followers.

The Greek is literally ‘kidneys and hearts’, echoing Jeremiah 17:10 and similar passages. In biblical idiom the kidneys are the seat of a person’s deepest feelings and motives. The claim is striking because the Old Testament says this of God alone.

notes.traditional: he shall rule them with a rod of iron
notes.note: The verb means to tend a flock and, by extension, to govern; most English versions render it ‘rule’. The wording follows the ancient Greek translation of Psalm 2:9, where the Hebrew text as traditionally read has ‘break’. ‘Shepherd’ keeps the word’s ordinary sense, though the context of an iron rod and shattered pottery shows that the shepherding is forceful.

candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the New Testament and translators divide between ‘church’, ‘assembly’ and ‘congregation’; readers would be misled if it varied between books.
Frequent across the Gospels, Acts and Revelation; ‘repent’ may suggest mere remorse where the Greek means a change of mind and course, so one policy is needed.
A key term in Revelation and the Johannine writings, rendered variously ‘overcome’, ‘conquer’ and ‘be victorious’; the refrain must be uniform across chapters 2–3 and beyond.
The verb and its noun πορνεία recur widely and are rendered ‘fornication’, ‘sexual immorality’ or ‘prostitution’; both the literal and the figurative uses need a consistent base rendering.
Very frequent, and the choice between ‘slave’ and ‘servant’ is a well-known dividing line among translations that must be settled once for the whole New Testament.
